Vignette:
A 12-year-old boy is brought to the office by his mother for a well-child checkup. The patient and his mother both state that the patient has been otherwise well except for occasional mild pain and stiffness in the upper back. Symptoms began gradually about a year ago and are present intermittently. The pain and stiffness do not bother him significantly or limit his activities, and they have never awakened him from sleep. He denies any trauma or overuse. He is not currently playing any organized sports although he is able to be normally active with friends and siblings.

Review of Systems:
General: Patient feels well except for occasional upper back pain and stiffness. No fever, chills, or night sweats. No weight loss or change in appetite. He is not yet shaving, and his voice has not yet changed.

Skin: Mild acne, no other rash or lesions.

HEENT: No vision changes, ear pain, hearing changes, neck stiffness, or pain in the throat.

Pulmonary: No shortness of breath or cough.

Cardiovascular: No chest pain or pressure.

Gastrointestinal: No diarrhea, vomiting, or abdominal pain. Normal bowel movement once a day.

Genitourinary: No dysuria or increased urinary frequency.

Musculoskeletal: Positive for intermittent upper back stiffness and discomfort. No joint swelling or discomfort.

Neurologic: No numbness, tingling, or pain running down his arms or legs. No weakness or gait changes. No difficulty controlling bladder or bowels.

Psychiatric: No depression, psychosis, or hyperactivity.

Past Medical History:
Medical history: Uncomplicated birth, no hospitalizations.

Surgical history: None

Medications: None

Allergies: Penicillin (rash)

Family history: His father had diabetes and hypertension and died when patient was very young. His maternal grandmother died of breast cancer at age 76 years. There is no history of skeletal dysplasia or muscular dystrophy in the family.

Social history: Patient was born at 37 weeks' gestation via spontaneous vaginal delivery and had an uncomplicated postnatal course. He is in age-appropriate grade in school and doing well academically and behaviorally. On interview with the mother outside the room, the patient reports that he feels happy and supported at home with his mother and sisters. Patient reports that he has never tried alcohol, drugs, or cigarettes. He is not sexually active.

The patient's family is from Guinea Bissau but the patient was born and raised in the United States and has not traveled outside the country. No known history of tuberculosis exposure. He is up to date on all vaccinations, and he received an influenza vaccine this year. He eats a normal diet, including fruits and vegetables, and drinks milk daily.

Physical Examination:
General appearance: African-American male child in no apparent discomfort, normal build and appearance.

Height: 160 cm (92nd percentile), Weight: 40 kgs (47th percentile)

Vital signs:
Temperature: 37° C
Pulse: 80 beats/min
BP: 105/66 mm Hg
Respirations: 16/min

Skin: No lesions or abnormal markings.

HEENT: Moist mucous membranes, normal dentition, no caries. Eye examination and vision normal bilaterally. Hearing grossly normal.

Pulmonary: Lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally. No chest deformity.

Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs, rubs, or gallops

Gastrointestinal: Abdomen soft, nontender, nondistended.

Genitourinary: Normal male genitalia Tanner Stage 3, testes descended bilaterally.

Musculoskeletal: Back has mild paraspinous tenderness bilaterally in the thoracic region. When patient bends forward at the waist with his arms hanging and palms together, his shoulders are not level and his scapulae appear asymmetric. Palpation of the spinous processes show slight right thoracic and left lumbar curvature. There is no leg-length discrepancy, and iliac crests are symmetrical. Extremities have full range of motion, no visible or palpable deformities or tenderness of extremities or joints.

Neurologic: Alert and oriented to person, place, and time. Normal patellar relaxes 2+ bilaterally, 5/5 motor strength in bilateral upper and lower extremities. Normal gait. No clonus. No strictures or rigidity in the extremities.

Mental status: Appropriate affect and behavior.

Test Results:
Results of appropriate testing return and show the following results:

X-ray of the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine:

No bony lesions noted. No signs of sacroiliitis. Scoliosis is present with right thoracic deviation and left lumbar deviation, Cobb angle 11°.

Focused musculoskeletal examination results:

Joint hypermobility: Absent
Ratio of upper body to lower body: 1.06
Ratio of wingspan to height: 0.98
baseline_protocol:
Age: 12  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Intermittent mild upper back pain and stiffness for one year, without functional limitation or red flag symptoms.  
Analysis: The patient presents with a chronic, mild, non-bothersome upper back pain and stiffness, beginning around the time of early adolescence. There are no red flags such as night pain, fever, weight loss, neurological deficits, bowel/bladder dysfunction, or trauma. Physical examination reveals truncal asymmetry, uneven shoulders, and asymmetric scapulae on forward bend test, with clinical and radiographic evidence of mild scoliosis (Cobb angle 11°). The curvature is right thoracic and left lumbar. The absence of neurological abnormalities, joint hypermobility, or systemic symptoms makes neuromuscular disease, inflammatory arthropathy, infection, or malignancy unlikely. Family history is negative for skeletal dysplasia or neuromuscular disorders. The patient is otherwise healthy, with normal pubertal development (Tanner Stage 3), normal growth parameters, and no psychosocial concerns. The mild paraspinous tenderness is likely musculoskeletal and related to postural strain from scoliosis. Given the Cobb angle <20°, absence of progression, and lack of symptoms interfering with function, this represents mild, stable idiopathic scoliosis.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: Mild adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (Cobb angle 11°) with minimal symptoms and no evidence of progression or underlying pathology; likely source of intermittent back discomfort.  
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics  
Recommendations: Reassure patient and family that the scoliosis is mild and does not require immediate intervention. Continue routine well-child care with annual monitoring of spinal curvature via physical exam (forward bend test) and serial height/weight tracking. Consider repeat X-ray in 6–12 months if growth spurt occurs or if clinical worsening is noted (e.g., increased asymmetry, pain progression). Encourage normal physical activity, including core-strengthening exercises (e.g., swimming, yoga) to support postural health. Avoid unnecessary imaging or bracing given current findings. Educate on signs of progression (e.g., visible hump, clothing fit changes, worsening pain, neurological symptoms) and when to return for re-evaluation.  
Notes: None

Vignette: A 19-year-old female college student is brought in by her roommate with a 24-hour history of high fever, diffuse rash, vomiting, profuse watery diarrhea, and progressive lightheadedness. She reports using a menstrual tampon that she forgot to change for approximately 3 days. On examination, she appears acutely ill with a diffuse, blanching, erythematous macular rash resembling a sunburn covering the trunk and extremities, including the palms and soles. Vital signs: T 40.2C, HR 136, RR 26, BP 72/40, SpO2 94%. Mucous membranes are hyperemic. Pelvic exam reveals a retained tampon, which is removed, and there is no evidence of abscess. Vignette:
A 19-year-old female college student is brought in by her roommate with a 24-hour history of high fever, diffuse rash, vomiting, profuse watery diarrhea, and progressive lightheadedness. She reports using a menstrual tampon that she forgot to change for approximately 3 days. On examination, she appears acutely ill with a diffuse, blanching, erythematous macular rash resembling a sunburn covering the trunk and extremities, including the palms and soles. Vital signs: T 40.2C, HR 136, RR 26, BP 72/40, SpO2 94%. Mucous membranes are hyperemic. Pelvic exam reveals a retained tampon, which is removed, and there is no evidence of abscess. Labs: WBC 15,400/mcL, platelets 88,000/mcL, creatinine 2.8 mg/dL, AST 245 U/L, ALT 198 U/L, CK 1,240 U/L. Blood cultures are drawn and empiric clindamycin and vancomycin are initiated.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 19  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: A 19-year-old female presents with 24 hours of high fever, diffuse macular rash, vomiting, profuse watery diarrhea, lightheadedness, and hypotension, following prolonged tampon use.  
Analysis: The clinical presentation is highly consistent with toxic shock syndrome (TSS), a toxin-mediated illness most commonly associated with Staphylococcus aureus and prolonged tampon use. Key findings include high fever (40.2°C), diffuse blanching erythematous rash involving palms and soles, hypotension (BP 72/40), multiorgan involvement (elevated creatinine, transaminitis, rhabdomyolysis with CK 1,240 U/L, thrombocytopenia), and mucous membrane hyperemia. The retained tampon serves as a likely nidus for toxin production. Differential diagnoses include streptococcal TSS, septic shock from another source, viral exanthem, or drug reaction; however, the temporal association with tampon use and classic clinical features make staphylococcal TSS the most likely diagnosis. Empiric antibiotics with clindamycin (toxin suppression) and vancomycin (MRSA coverage) are appropriate.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: This patient presents with classic signs and laboratory findings of toxic shock syndrome likely due to prolonged tampon retention, resulting in systemic inflammation, hypotension, and multiorgan dysfunction.  
Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Infectious Disease  
Recommendations:  
- Immediate ICU admission for hemodynamic monitoring and support.  
- Aggressive fluid resuscitation with crystalloids for septic shock.  
- Continue empiric clindamycin and vancomycin; consider adding antistaphylococcal penicillin (e.g., nafcillin) if culture confirms MSSA.  
- Initiate vasopressors (e.g., norepinephrine) if hypotension persists after fluid resuscitation.  
- Monitor urine output, lactate, and organ function closely.  
- Ensure source control: retained tampon has been removed—no further surgical intervention needed unless complications arise.  
- Consider IV immunoglobulin (IVIG) in severe cases to neutralize superantigens, especially if refractory shock.  
- Rule out other sources of infection (e.g., wound, post-surgical); blood cultures pending.  
- Provide supportive care including electrolyte management, renal monitoring, and dermatologic care for desquamation (expected in 1–2 weeks).

- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case

criterion:
Step 1:Does the Analysis field make the reasoning from the case findings to the Conclusion traceable?  The key findings that actually support the stated conclusion must be named, and the Analysis must make clear why they support that conclusion rather than merely listing case facts or restating the diagnosis. Where the protocol raises competing explanations it must say what makes the chosen one more likely rather than leaving them side by side. A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.
Step 2: Are the fields of the protocol mutually consistent? The Complaint, Analysis, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Required diagnostic equipment/tests and Recommendations must not contradict one another. Examples of contradictions: an Emergency type of self-care alongside a recommendation to attend the emergency department, a Conclusion naming one condition while the Recommendations manage another, a Subclinical specialization that does not correspond to the condition concluded, or a test listed as required whose result the Analysis already assumes. If they contradict, fail.
A conditional assessment, that is, one that lays out more than one scenario, is not a failure of this criterion, provided the conditions themselves follow from the case.
Judge only the logical connection between the case findings and the stated conclusion and the internal consistency of the protocol

tags: ['axis:urgency']
criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:uncertainty']
criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

tags: ['axis:communication_quality']
criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

Vignette:
A 6-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents after 8 hours of progressive wheezing and respiratory distress despite using his albuterol inhaler every 20 minutes at home. He has a history of moderate persistent asthma with two prior ICU admissions. He recently had an upper respiratory infection. On examination, he is sitting upright, using accessory muscles, and speaking in single words only. Vital signs: T 37.8C, HR 152, RR 42, BP 100/65, SpO2 87% on room air. Lung auscultation reveals markedly diminished breath sounds bilaterally with minimal wheezing, suggesting severe air trapping. Peak flow is unobtainable due to patient fatigue. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.28, pCO2 55 mmHg.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 6  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: 6-year-old boy with 8 hours of progressive wheezing and respiratory distress despite frequent albuterol use, now with signs of severe respiratory compromise.  
Analysis: The patient presents with acute severe asthma exacerbation complicated by impending respiratory failure. Key findings include use of accessory muscles, inability to speak more than single words, markedly diminished breath sounds with minimal wheezing (suggesting severe air trapping and poor air movement), hypoxemia (SpO2 87% on room air), tachycardia, tachypnea, and venous blood gas showing respiratory acidosis (pH 7.28, pCO2 55 mmHg). These are indicators of alveolar hypoventilation and fatigue, placing the patient at high risk for respiratory arrest. History of moderate persistent asthma and prior ICU admissions further increases risk. Differential considerations include status asthmaticus (primary diagnosis), foreign body aspiration (less likely given bilateral findings and history), and pneumonia (possible but less likely given predominant wheezing and asthma history), though none override the clear picture of severe asthma exacerbation.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: This child is in severe respiratory distress with clinical and blood gas evidence of impending respiratory failure due to status asthmaticus. Immediate intervention is required to prevent respiratory arrest.  
Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Pulmonology  
Recommendations:  
- Administer high-flow oxygen to maintain SpO2 ≥94%.  
- Initiate continuous albuterol (15 mg/hour) via heated nebulizer with ipratropium bromide (0.5 mg every 20 minutes for 3 doses, then as needed).  
- Give systemic corticosteroids immediately: dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg (max 10 mg) PO/IV or prednisone 1–2 mg/kg (max 60 mg).  
- Administer IV magnesium sulfate: 50 mg/kg (max 2 g) over 20 minutes.  
- Establish IV access and monitor cardiac rhythm, oxygen saturation, and respiratory effort continuously.  
- Avoid sedatives. Prepare for noninvasive ventilation (e.g., BiPAP) if work of breathing persists or worsens despite initial therapy.  
- If there is no rapid improvement or if mental status declines, prepare for immediate intubation and mechanical ventilation by experienced personnel.  
- Admit to pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) given history of prior ICU admissions and current severity.  

Notes: Diminished breath sounds in the setting of severe asthma may be misinterpreted as improvement but actually indicate minimal air movement and high risk of respiratory failure. Rising pCO2 in the context of asthma is a late and ominous sign.

A 53-yr-old woman comes to the office because of palpitations. She is a current patient there
and has a history of well-controlled hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and tension headaches. She
states that she has noticed intermittent palpitations over the past 2 mo. She describes the
episodes as a sensation of irregular and racing heartbeats that are accompanied by fatigue.
She denies any chest pain, shortness of breath, light-headedness, or syncope. The episodes
last from 10 min to several hours, occur once or twice/wk, and resolve on their own. The last
episode was 3 days ago. She cannot identify any particular triggers. She is generally active and
walks 3 miles several days/wk without any exertional symptoms including chest pain and
dyspnea. She has no family history of early cardiac disease or sudden death. She denies any
recent fever or infectious symptoms.

Vignette:
A 53-yr-old woman comes to the office because of palpitations. She is a current patient there

episodes as a sensation of irregular and racing heartbeats that are accompanied by fatigue.
She denies any chest pain, shortness of breath, light-headedness, or syncope. The episodes
last from 10 min to several hours, occur once or twice/wk, and resolve on their own. The last
episode was 3 days ago. She cannot identify any particular triggers. She is generally active and
walks 3 miles several days/wk without any exertional symptoms including chest pain and
dyspnea. She has no family history of early cardiac disease or sudden death. She denies any
recent fever or infectious symptoms.

HEENT: No vision changes, ear pain, nasal symptoms, or sore throat.

Gastrointestinal: Denies abdominal pain and poor appetite.

Genitourinary: Noncontributory

Reproductive: Noncontributory

Musculoskeletal: No recent injury.

Neurologic: Noncontributory

Medical history: Hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and tension headaches.

Medications: Lisinopril 10 mg daily and metformin 500 mg bid.

cancer. No history of early coronary artery disease or sudden cardiac death.

Age: 53  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Intermittent palpitations over the past 2 months, described as irregular and racing heartbeats, associated with fatigue; no chest pain, dyspnea, lightheadedness, or syncope.  
Analysis: The patient is a 53-year-old woman with well-controlled hypertension and type 2 diabetes presenting with intermittent palpitations characterized by irregular and rapid heartbeats lasting 10 minutes to several hours, occurring 1–2 times per week. The absence of red-flag symptoms such as syncope, exertional chest pain, dyspnea, or orthostatic symptoms reduces immediate concern for life-threatening arrhythmias or structural heart disease. Physical examination reveals a slow resting heart rate (58 bpm) but otherwise normal cardiovascular findings with no signs of heart failure or valvular disease. Given the episodic and self-resolving nature of symptoms, the most likely differential includes paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT) or atrial fibrillation/flutter. Other considerations include sinus arrhythmia or non-cardiac causes such as anxiety or stimulant use; however, the patient denies stress extremes, caffeine excess, or stimulant use. Her regular alcohol intake (daily wine) may contribute, though no clear trigger is identified. The normal exam and lack of family history of sudden cardiac death or early coronary artery disease further support a lower-risk profile.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Resting 12-lead electrocardiogram, ambulatory rhythm monitoring (e.g., 24–48 hour Holter or 14-day event monitor), thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), complete blood count (CBC), basic metabolic panel (BMP) including potassium and magnesium.  
Conclusion: Intermittent palpitations in a middle-aged woman with controlled cardiometabolic risk factors, no red-flag symptoms, and normal physical examination. Likely arrhythmic etiology requiring rhythm correlation during episodes; no evidence of acute cardiac decompensation or high-risk features.  
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: General Medicine  
Recommendations:  
- Perform resting ECG to assess baseline rhythm, QT interval, and for signs of conduction abnormalities or prior ischemia.  
- Initiate ambulatory ECG monitoring (preferably extended 14-day event monitor given episodic nature and last episode 3 days ago) to capture arrhythmia during symptoms.  
- Order TSH to rule out hyperthyroidism as a contributing factor; check CBC for anemia and BMP for electrolyte imbalances (e.g., hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia).  
- Counsel on moderate alcohol intake (consider temporary reduction to assess symptom correlation).  
- Continue current medications (lisinopril, metformin); no indication for change.  
- Avoid unnecessary stimulants; confirm no over-the-counter decongestant use.  
- Follow up in clinic to review test results and determine need for cardiology referral based on monitoring outcome.  
Notes: None

A 72-year-old woman presents with generalized dry, itchy skin that has been worsening over the past several weeks as winter has progressed. She reports the itching is worst on her shins and forearms. baseline_protocol:
Age: 72  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Generalized dry, itchy skin worsening in winter, most severe on shins and forearms.  
Analysis: The patient presents with typical features of asteatotic change (xerosis cutis) in an older adult during winter, exacerbated by frequent hot bathing and use of harsh bar soap. Clinical findings include fine scaling, superficial cracking, and a "cracked pavement" appearance on the shins and forearms—classic for asteatotic eczema. The absence of primary inflammatory lesions (papules, plaques), excoriations, lymphadenopathy, or systemic symptoms (jaundice, weight loss) argues against inflammatory dermatoses (e.g., cutaneous lymphoma, bullous pemphigoid prodrome), scabies, or systemic disease. The seasonal pattern and bathing habits strongly support environmentally induced xerosis.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: Asteatotic eczema (eczema craquelé) secondary to environmental dryness and improper skin care practices in an elderly patient.  
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology  
Recommendations:  
- Discontinue hot baths and regular bar soap; recommend lukewarm water and gentle, fragrance-free cleansers (e.g., syndet bars or lipid-free cleansers).  
- Apply thick emollients (e.g., petrolatum, ceramide-based creams) immediately after bathing and multiple times daily.  
- Use a humidifier indoors to counteract winter dryness.  
- Avoid scratching; wear soft, non-irritating clothing.  
- If pruritus persists despite moisturization, consider short-term use of low-potency topical corticosteroid (e.g., hydrocortisone 1%) on most affected areas for 7–10 days.  
- Reassess in 2–4 weeks if no improvement, to rule out underlying dermatitis or other conditions.  
Notes: None

Vignette:
A 20-year-old female college student who recently started a running program presents with bilateral dull, aching pain along the front of both shins. The pain began about 1 week ago and occurs primarily during and shortly after running, then resolves with rest. She runs on paved surfaces in her current athletic shoes that are over a year old. She denies pain at rest, nighttime pain, swelling, or history of stress fractures. On examination, there is mild tenderness on palpation along the medial border of the bilateral tibias spanning approximately 5 cm. There is no point tenderness, edema, or erythema. Ankle range of motion and strength are normal.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 20  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Bilateral dull, aching shin pain that occurs during and shortly after running, resolving with rest, with tenderness along the medial tibial border.  
Analysis: The patient is a young female with recent initiation of a running program who presents with bilateral, exertional shin pain localized to the medial tibial border, lasting during and immediately after activity and resolving with rest. Tenderness spans approximately 5 cm along the posteromedial tibia bilaterally without point tenderness, edema, or erythema. These features are classic for medial tibial stress syndrome (MTSS), also known as "shin splints." The absence of pain at rest, nighttime pain, or point tenderness makes tibial stress fracture less likely. Normal ankle strength and range of motion argue against significant neuromuscular or joint pathology. Chronic exertional compartment syndrome typically presents with progressive pain during exercise that persists for minutes after stopping and may include tightness, paresthesia, or weakness, which are absent here. There is no evidence of vascular compromise or popliteal artery entrapment. Nerve entrapment is unlikely given the bilateral, symmetric presentation and lack of neurological findings. Risk factors include running on hard surfaces and use of worn footwear (>1 year old), which may contribute to increased impact loading.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: The clinical presentation is consistent with medial tibial stress syndrome, likely due to recent increase in running activity on hard surfaces with inadequate footwear.  
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics  
Recommendations:  
- Relative rest:暂停 running during acute phase; switch to non-impact cross-training (e.g., swimming, cycling, elliptical) to maintain cardiovascular fitness.  
- Replace running shoes with new, supportive footwear designed for running, considering gait analysis if symptoms recur.  
- Gradual return to running using a structured, progressive program (e.g., walk-run intervals) only after pain-free daily activities.  
- Address biomechanical factors: avoid running on hard surfaces when possible; consider evaluation for overpronation or flat feet if symptoms persist.  
- Ice and NSAIDs as needed for symptom relief, though not required long-term.  
- Monitor for red flags: development of focal, persistent pain at rest, point tenderness, or worsening symptoms, which would warrant imaging (e.g., MRI) to rule out stress fracture.  

Notes: None

Complaint: Acute acetaminophen overdose with nausea, vomiting, right upper quadrant abdominal pain, and elevated transaminases 12 hours post-ingestion.  
Analysis: The patient presents with a clear history of intentional ingestion of approximately 25 grams of acetaminophen (50 tablets of 500 mg), a toxic dose exceeding 150 mg/kg. At 12 hours post-ingestion, she exhibits symptoms of early hepatotoxicity including nausea, vomiting, and right upper quadrant pain. Laboratory findings confirm acute liver injury: markedly elevated AST and ALT (>1000 U/L), elevated INR (1.8), and mild hyperbilirubinemia (2.1 mg/dL), all consistent with stage 2 or early stage 3 of acetaminophen toxicity. The acetaminophen serum level of 180 mcg/mL at 12 hours is well above the treatment line on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram, confirming the need for antidotal therapy. Metabolic acidosis is mild (pH 7.34, lactate 2.8 mmol/L), possibly reflecting early hepatic dysfunction or mild volume depletion. Scleral icterus is absent, indicating early progression. Differential considerations include other causes of acute hepatitis (e.g., viral, autoimmune), but the temporal relationship to ingestion and classic lab pattern strongly support acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: This is a case of acute, intentional acetaminophen overdose resulting in early, significant hepatotoxicity, requiring immediate medical intervention and multidisciplinary management.  
Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Emergency

Vignette:
A 70-year-old man presents with 18 hours of worsening right upper quadrant pain, fever with rigors, and progressive yellowing of his skin and eyes. He has a history of choledocholithiasis with a prior ERCP and sphincterotomy 5 years ago. On examination, he appears jaundiced and acutely ill with intermittent rigors. Vital signs: T 39.6C, HR 118, RR 22, BP 88/52, SpO2 96%. Abdominal examination reveals significant right upper quadrant tenderness with a positive Murphy sign. Scleral icterus is prominent. Labs: WBC 22,600/mcL with 15% bands, total bilirubin 8.4 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 6.8 mg/dL, ALP 482 U/L, AST 188 U/L, ALT 162 U/L, lipase normal, lactate 4.1 mmol/L. Blood cultures are drawn. Right upper quadrant ultrasound shows common bile duct dilation to 14 mm with a shadowing stone in the distal CBD and mild intrahepatic ductal dilation.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 70  
Sex: Not specified  
Complaint: 18 hours of worsening right upper quadrant pain, fever with rigors, and jaundice in a patient with prior choledocholithiasis.  
Analysis: The clinical presentation is consistent with acute cholangitis, characterized by Charcot’s triad (right upper quadrant pain, fever, jaundice) and progressing to Reynolds’ pentad with hypotension and altered mental status (implied by acutely ill appearance and shock). Key findings include high fever (39.6°C), tachycardia (HR 118), hypotension (BP 88/52), leukocytosis with bandemia (WBC 22,600/mcL, 15% bands), elevated bilirubin (direct > indirect), elevated ALP and transaminases, and lactic acidosis (lactate 4.1 mmol/L), indicating systemic inflammatory response and end-organ hypoperfusion. Imaging confirms common bile duct dilation (14 mm) with a distal CBD stone and mild intrahepatic ductal dilation, consistent with obstructive cholangiopathy. Differential diagnoses include acute cholecystitis, acute hepatitis, and sepsis from other sources, but the combination of biliary obstruction on imaging, prior sphincterotomy, and lab evidence of cholestasis strongly favors cholangitis due to choledocholithiasis.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: This is a case of acute cholangitis secondary to choledocholithiasis with biliary obstruction and early septic shock, requiring immediate biliary decompression and resuscitation.  
Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Gastroenterology  
Recommendations:  
1. Immediate resuscitation with IV crystalloids to address hypotension and lactic acidosis.  
2. Start broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics (e.g., piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem) to cover gram-negative and anaerobic organisms.  
3. Admit to hospital with intensive monitoring; consider ICU if shock progresses.  
4. Urgent endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) within 24 hours (preferably <12 hours given severity) for biliary decompression and stone removal.  
5. Maintain NPO status pending ERCP.  
6. Monitor renal function, electrolytes, and lactate trends.  
7. Blood cultures already drawn—ensure timely follow-up for pathogen identification and antibiotic de-escalation.  
Notes: Delay in biliary decompression increases mortality in severe cholangitis; early ERCP is the cornerstone of definitive management. Surgical consultation may be needed if ERCP is unavailable or unsuccessful.

The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.
The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,
- "None" is used for a field that this case clearly requires, for example no further workup is proposed although the conclusion is not yet established.
Do not fail a field merely because information that properly belongs in another field is not duplicated there.
Judge only whether the required content is present. The medical correctness of the content that is present is graded elsewhere, and so is the wording in which expectations are conveyed to the patient.

[3]
tags: ['axis:reasoning']
criterion:
Step 1:Does the Analysis field make the reasoning from the case findings to the Conclusion traceable?  The key findings that actually support the stated conclusion must be named, and the Analysis must make clear why they support that conclusion rather than merely listing case facts or restating the diagnosis. Where the protocol raises competing explanations it must say what makes the chosen one more likely rather than leaving them side by side. A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.
Step 2: Are the fields of the protocol mutually consistent? The Complaint, Analysis, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Required diagnostic equipment/tests and Recommendations must not contradict one another. Examples of contradictions: an Emergency type of self-care alongside a recommendation to attend the emergency department, a Conclusion naming one condition while the Recommendations manage another, a Subclinical specialization that does not correspond to the condition concluded, or a test listed as required whose result the Analysis already assumes. If they contradict, fail.
A conditional assessment, that is, one that lays out more than one scenario, is not a failure of this criterion, provided the conditions themselves follow from the case.
Judge only the logical connection between the case findings and the stated conclusion and the internal consistency of the protocol
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:urgency']
criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:uncertainty']
criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

tags: ['axis:communication_quality']
criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

Vignette:
A 3-year-old girl is brought in by her mother with a low-grade fever of 37.8°C and small blisters noticed on her hands and feet since this morning. The mother also notes a few small sores inside the child's mouth. The child is eating and drinking well, though slightly fussier than usual. Several children at her daycare have had similar symptoms. On examination, there are scattered small vesicles on the palms, soles, and a few on the dorsal hands. Two shallow ulcers are seen on the buccal mucosa. The child is alert, playful, and well-hydrated.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 3 years  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Low-grade fever, oral ulcers, and vesicles on hands and feet in a daycare-attending child with similar cases reported.  
Analysis: The clinical presentation of low-grade fever, oral mucosal ulcers, and vesicles on the palms, soles, and dorsal hands is classic for hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD), most commonly caused by coxsackievirus A16 or enterovirus 71. The presence of multiple affected children in the same daycare supports a contagious viral etiology with fecal-oral and respiratory droplet transmission. The child is well-hydrated, alert, playful, and able to eat and drink, which indicates a mild course. Key differentials include herpangina (which primarily presents with posterior oral ulcers without skin involvement) and herpetic gingivostomatitis (typically with more severe oral pain, gingival inflammation, and no palmar/plantar vesicles). The distribution and mild systemic symptoms strongly favor HFMD.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: Mild, typical presentation of hand, foot, and mouth disease in a preschool-aged child, likely enteroviral in origin, with no signs of complications.  
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: Infectious Disease  
Recommendations: Advise symptomatic management including hydration, soft cool foods, and analgesia with acetaminophen or ibuprofen as needed. Emphasize strict hand hygiene, especially after diaper changes, and disinfection of shared toys and surfaces in the home and daycare. Exclude the child from daycare until fever has resolved and vesicles have dried (typically 7–10 days), per local public health guidelines. Educate parents that viral shedding in stool may continue for weeks after symptom resolution, necessitating ongoing hygiene. Counsel that pregnant staff or household contacts should practice careful hygiene due to theoretical (though rare) risks of vertical transmission with enteroviruses. Notify public health authorities only if there is a large or severe cluster, or signs of unusual complications.  
Notes: None

Vignette:
A 68-yr-old woman comes to the office with her daughter because of a 4-mo history of gradually
increasing lethargy and worsening memory. Her daughter is concerned because the mother has
stopped remembering whether she has taken her regular medications. The daughter is worried
that her mother might not be safe to live on her own. Prior to 4 mo ago, the woman had been
very busy with community activities, which she has since stopped, and her daughter had not
noticed any memory difficulties. The daughter is not aware of any recent illnesses or injuries.
Review of Systems:
General: The patient says she feels tired all the time and is usually cold even now during the
summer. She has a poor appetite but has gained 5 kg in weight in the preceding 4 mo despite
decreased appetite. No fever, chills, headache, or body aches.

Skin: Her skin has become dry, and her hair is now coarse and sparse. No rash or itching.

HEENT: She reports fullness in her throat, and her daughter has noticed that her mother's
voice has become hoarse and her face appears puffy, particularly around the eyes. No difficulty
swallowing.

Pulmonary: The patient reports new exertional shortness of breath and needing to pause after
climbing 1/2 flight of stairs. No cough or wheezing.

Cardiovascular: She used to have occasional palpitations before but has had none for the last 2
mo. She denies chest pain, orthopnea, or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea.

Gastrointestinal: The patient's bowel movements have decreased from daily to once every 3
to 4 days when using laxatives. She does not have any abdominal pain or vomiting. Her
appetite is decreased.

Genitourinary: Noncontributory

Musculoskeletal: Her ankles and lower legs are more swollen than they used to be. She reports
fatigue and leg weakness when climbing stairs or getting up from a chair.

Neurologic: She has become slower at performing daily activities, and extra effort is required.
Her daughter has noticed that her mother has trouble remembering recent events, such as
whether she has taken her medications. She denies having focal weakness or sensory
abnormalities, tremor, or visual symptoms.

Psychiatric: Her mood is depressed and she often stays in bed, not going out of the house for
many days.
Past Medical History:
Medical history: Hypertension diagnosed 10 yr ago and controlled with three antihypertensives.
Atrial fibrillation (AF) rate-controlled with bisoprolol; previous admission to hospital with a fast
AF complicated with acute left ventricular failure; cardioversion failed to restore sinus rhythm.

Surgical history: Appendectomy at the age of 19 yr, left carpal tunnel syndrome surgery 2 yr
ago.

Medications: Bisoprolol 5 mg once/day, ramipril 10 mg once/day, furosemide 40 mg once/day,
warfarin 3 mg once/day.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

Family history: Mother had hypothyroidism and a stroke in her 80s. Father died of metastatic
colon cancer.

Social history: She eats a healthy balanced diet, and her only exercise is walking to nearby
shops twice a week. She used to work as a receptionist but retired 3 yr ago. She is a
nonsmoker and drinks alcohol only occasionally. She has not travelled abroad in the last 3 yr.

General appearance: The patient is wearing several layers of clothing including a wool sweater

Respirations: 16/min

Vignette:
A 68-yr-old woman comes to the office with her daughter because of a 4-mo history of gradually
increasing lethargy and worsening memory. Her daughter is concerned because the mother has
stopped remembering whether she has taken her regular medications. The daughter is worried
that her mother might not be safe to live on her own. Prior to 4 mo ago, the woman had been
very busy with community activities, which she has since stopped, and her daughter had not
noticed any memory difficulties. The daughter is not aware of any recent illnesses or injuries.

Review of Systems:
General: The patient says she feels tired all the time and is usually cold even now during the
summer. She has a poor appetite but has gained 5 kg in weight in the preceding 4 mo despite
decreased appetite. No fever, chills, headache, or body aches.

Skin: Her skin has become dry, and her hair is now coarse and sparse. No rash or itching.

HEENT: She reports fullness in her throat, and her daughter has noticed that her mother's
voice has become hoarse and her face appears puffy, particularly around the eyes. No difficulty
swallowing.

Pulmonary: The patient reports new exertional shortness of breath and needing to pause after
climbing 1/2 flight of stairs. No cough or wheezing.

Cardiovascular: She used to have occasional palpitations before but has had none for the last 2
mo. She denies chest pain, orthopnea, or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea.

Gastrointestinal: The patient's bowel movements have decreased from daily to once every 3
to 4 days when using laxatives. She does not have any abdominal pain or vomiting. Her
appetite is decreased.

Genitourinary: Noncontributory

Musculoskeletal: Her ankles and lower legs are more swollen than they used to be. She reports
fatigue and leg weakness when climbing stairs or getting up from a chair.

Neurologic: She has become slower at performing daily activities, and extra effort is required.
Her daughter has noticed that her mother has trouble remembering recent events, such as
whether she has taken her medications. She denies having focal weakness or sensory
abnormalities, tremor, or visual symptoms.

Psychiatric: Her mood is depressed and she often stays in bed, not going out of the house for
many days.

Past Medical History:
Medical history: Hypertension diagnosed 10 yr ago and controlled with three antihypertensives.
Atrial fibrillation (AF) rate-controlled with bisoprolol; previous admission to hospital with a fast
AF complicated with acute left ventricular failure; cardioversion failed to restore sinus rhythm.

Surgical history: Appendectomy at the age of 19 yr, left carpal tunnel syndrome surgery 2 yr
ago.

Medications: Bisoprolol 5 mg once/day, ramipril 10 mg once/day, furosemide 40 mg once/day,
warfarin 3 mg once/day.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

Family history: Mother had hypothyroidism and a stroke in her 80s. Father died of metastatic
colon cancer.

Social history: She eats a healthy balanced diet, and her only exercise is walking to nearby
shops twice a week. She used to work as a receptionist but retired 3 yr ago. She is a
nonsmoker and drinks alcohol only occasionally. She has not travelled abroad in the last 3 yr.

General appearance: The patient is wearing several layers of clothing including a wool sweater
despite it being 89° F outside. She has a dull facial expression, and she looks pale and tired.

Temperature: 35.8° C
Pulse: 56 beats/min, irregular
BP: 120/90 mm Hg
Respirations: 16/min

baseline_protocol:
Age: 68  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: A 68-year-old woman presents with 4 months of progressive lethargy, memory decline, cold intolerance, weight gain despite poor appetite, constipation, hoarseness, periorbital and lower extremity edema, and slowing of physical and mental function.  

Analysis: The clinical presentation is highly suggestive of primary hypothyroidism. Key findings include fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, dry skin, coarse hair, eyebrow loss, periorbital edema, hoarse voice, bradycardia, delayed deep tendon reflexes, proximal muscle weakness, depression, and cognitive slowing. Laboratory results confirm marked elevation in TSH (88 µIU/mL) and low free T4 (0.4 ng/dL), diagnostic of primary hypothyroidism. Positive thyroid peroxidase antibodies (258 IU/mL) support autoimmune thyroiditis (Hashimoto’s thyroiditis) as the underlying etiology. The presence of a firm, nontender goiter and family history of hypothyroidism further supports this diagnosis. The patient's atrial fibrillation, now controlled, may have been previously influenced by thyroid dysfunction. Anemia (Hb 9.8 g/dL) is likely multifactorial but commonly associated with hypothyroidism. Other findings such as bibasilar crackles, mild cardiomegaly on CXR, and leg edema may reflect hypothyroidism-related fluid retention or pre-existing cardiac disease. Differential diagnoses such as depression, dementia, heart failure, or malignancy are less likely given the global metabolic symptoms and definitive lab abnormalities pointing to hypothyroidism.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  

Conclusion: This patient has symptomatic primary hypothyroidism due to autoimmune thyroiditis, complicated by anemia and likely contributing to her cognitive, neuromuscular, cardiovascular, and metabolic symptoms.  

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  

Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology  

Recommendations:  
- Initiate levothyroxine replacement therapy at a low dose (e.g., 25–50 mcg daily) due to patient’s age and history of atrial fibrillation with prior heart failure, to avoid cardiac strain.  
- Monitor thyroid function (TSH, free T4) every 6–8 weeks after initiation and with each dose adjustment until target TSH is achieved (typically 0.5–4.5 µIU/mL).  
- Titrate levothyroxine dose gradually (e.g., increase by 12.5–25 mcg every 4–6 weeks) based on response and tolerance.  
- Evaluate and manage coexisting anemia: consider iron studies, vitamin B12, and folate levels; rule out gastrointestinal causes given constipation and left iliac fossa discomfort.  
- Assess for other autoimmune conditions (e.g., pernicious anemia, adrenal insufficiency) given positive TPO antibodies and family history.  
- Re-evaluate cognitive and functional status after thyroid hormone normalization; avoid premature labeling as dementia.  
- Continue current medications with close monitoring; bisoprolol may mask tachycardia but does not preclude cautious levothyroxine use.  
- Counsel patient and family about expected gradual improvement in symptoms over weeks to months.  

Notes: None

baseline_protocol:
Age: 9 months  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Episodic inconsolable crying with leg drawing, vomiting, and currant jelly stool in a 9-month-old infant.  
Analysis: The clinical presentation is classic for intussusception, including paroxysmal abdominal pain, vomiting, lethargy, and passage of currant jelly stool. Key physical findings include a palpable sausage-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant, an empty right lower quadrant (Dance sign), and abdominal distension. The presence of pallor, tachycardia (HR 168), and borderline hypotension (BP 80/52) suggests early compensated shock, likely due to pain and/or dehydration. The recent viral upper respiratory infection may be a potential trigger, as intussusception is often preceded by viral illness. The diagnosis is confirmed by abdominal ultrasound showing the target sign (doughnut sign) consistent with ileocolic intussusception, with no signs of perforation or peritonitis. Differential diagnoses such as gastroenteritis, sepsis, malrotation with volvulus, and appendicitis are less likely given the classic imaging and clinical features.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: A 9-month-old male with confirmed ileocolic intussusception presenting with classic symptoms and signs, including currant jelly stool, palpable abdominal mass, and ultrasound-confirmed target sign, without evidence of perforation.  
Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: General Surgery  
Recommendations: Proceed immediately with non-surgical reduction using air enema under radiologic guidance, as the patient is hemodynamically stable without signs of peritonitis or perforation. Ensure intravenous access is established, and initiate fluid resuscitation to address tachycardia and borderline hypotension. Monitor closely for signs of deterioration, including worsening abdominal pain, peritonitis, or hemodynamic instability, which would necessitate surgical intervention. If air enema reduction fails or perforation occurs, emergent surgical consultation and possible laparotomy are indicated.  
Notes: Success rates for air enema reduction are high when performed early and in the absence of complications. Post-reduction, observe for recurrence, bleeding, or signs of perforation.

The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.
The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,
- "None" is used for a field that this case clearly requires, for example no further workup is proposed although the conclusion is not yet established.
Do not fail a field merely because information that properly belongs in another field is not duplicated there.
Judge only whether the required content is present. The medical correctness of the content that is present is graded elsewhere, and so is the wording in which expectations are conveyed to the patient.

criterion:
Step 1:Does the Analysis field make the reasoning from the case findings to the Conclusion traceable?  The key findings that actually support the stated conclusion must be named, and the Analysis must make clear why they support that conclusion rather than merely listing case facts or restating the diagnosis. Where the protocol raises competing explanations it must say what makes the chosen one more likely rather than leaving them side by side. A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.
Step 2: Are the fields of the protocol mutually consistent? The Complaint, Analysis, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Required diagnostic equipment/tests and Recommendations must not contradict one another. Examples of contradictions: an Emergency type of self-care alongside a recommendation to attend the emergency department, a Conclusion naming one condition while the Recommendations manage another, a Subclinical specialization that does not correspond to the condition concluded, or a test listed as required whose result the Analysis already assumes. If they contradict, fail.
A conditional assessment, that is, one that lays out more than one scenario, is not a failure of this criterion, provided the conditions themselves follow from the case.
Judge only the logical connection between the case findings and the stated conclusion and the internal consistency of the protocol
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

case_text:
Vignette:
A 70-year-old man with a history of benign prostatic hyperplasia presents to his primary care physician with a 3-day history of dysuria, urinary frequency, and urgency. He reports mild suprapubic discomfort and low-grade fever of 100.4°F. He denies flank pain, rigors, or hematuria. His past medical history is notable for BPH managed with tamsulosin. On examination, he appears mildly uncomfortable but is in no acute distress. Vital signs show temperature 100.4°F, blood pressure 138/82, heart rate 78. Abdominal examination reveals mild suprapubic tenderness without guarding. Digital rectal exam shows an enlarged, nontender prostate. Urinalysis demonstrates pyuria and positive nitrites.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 70  
Sex: Not specified  
Complaint: A 70-year-old man presents with 3 days of dysuria, urinary frequency, urgency, mild suprapubic discomfort, and low-grade fever.  
Analysis: The patient has symptoms and urinalysis findings consistent with acute bacterial lower urinary tract infection (cystitis). Key findings include dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic tenderness, pyuria, and positive nitrites, which are highly suggestive of urinary tract infection. The absence of flank pain, costovertebral angle tenderness, rigors, or high fever makes pyelonephritis less likely. The enlarged, nontender prostate on digital rectal exam in the context of known BPH suggests benign prostatic enlargement rather than acute bacterial prostatitis, which typically presents with a tender, warm, and boggy prostate. Hematuria is denied, and there are no systemic signs of sepsis. Given his age and underlying BPH, he is at increased risk for complicated urinary tract infection.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: This is a likely case of acute uncomplicated cystitis in a man with underlying benign prostatic hyperplasia; however, due to male sex and age, it should be managed as a complicated UTI.  
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Urology  
Recommendations: Initiate empiric antibiotic therapy for complicated UTI (e.g., nitrofurantoin if renal function is normal and no contraindications, or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole if local resistance patterns allow; alternatively, consider fluoroquinolone such as ciprofloxacin given complexity). Obtain urine culture prior to starting antibiotics to guide therapy. Advise increased fluid intake and monitor for worsening symptoms (e.g., fever, flank pain, hematuria, or inability to void). Follow up within 1–2 days to assess response. Consider urology referral if recurrent infections, poor response, or concern for obstructive uropathy. Avoid anticholinergics that may worsen urinary retention.  
Notes: In older men with BPH, even mild UTI symptoms warrant culture and careful follow-up due to risk of complications such as prostatic abscess or upper tract involvement. Pyuria and positive nitrites support infection but do not exclude other causes; if symptoms persist despite treatment, further evaluation (e.g., imaging, cystoscopy) may be needed.

baseline_protocol:
Age: 66  
Sex: Woman  
Complaint: Progressive abdominal distension, crampy abdominal pain, bilious and feculent vomiting, and failure to pass flatus or stool for 36 hours.  
Analysis: The clinical presentation is consistent with a high-grade small bowel obstruction, supported by abdominal distension, tympany, high-pitched bowel sounds, and absence of flatus or bowel movements. Key imaging findings include dilated small bowel loops (up to 5.2 cm), a transition point in the right lower quadrant, small bowel feces sign, and possible closed-loop configuration—findings highly suggestive of mechanical obstruction with concern for closed-loop anatomy, which increases the risk of strangulation. Surgical history (appendectomy and hysterectomy) increases the likelihood of adhesive disease, though the right lower quadrant transition point may suggest other etiologies such as hernia or chronic adhesion band. Elevated WBC, lactate, and renal parameters suggest systemic stress and possible early ischemia. The combination of pain, distension, vomiting, obstetric history, and concerning CT findings rules out paralytic ileus and supports mechanical obstruction with possible complications.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: Acute small bowel obstruction with imaging features concerning for closed-loop configuration and possible early ischemia, likely adhesive or post-surgical in origin.  
Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: General Surgery  
Recommendations: Immediate surgical consultation for suspected small bowel obstruction with closed-loop features. Initiate NPO, nasogastric tube decompression, intravenous fluid resuscitation, and broad-spectrum antibiotics given elevated lactate and WBC. Monitor for signs of peritonitis or clinical deterioration. Prepare for possible emergent laparotomy given concern for strangulation. Avoid oral or intravenous contrast due to high-grade obstruction.  
Notes: Closed-loop obstruction is a surgical emergency; delay increases risk of bowel ischemia and perforation.
